requirements.heading: Basic Structure
requirements.text: In many situations and configurations, the less- capable clients discussed above SHOULD be using the message submission protocol (RFC 4409 [18]) rather than SMTP.

requirements.heading: Basic Structure
requirements.text: In either case, once the server has issued a success response at the end of the mail data, a formal handoff of responsibility for the message occurs: the protocol requires that a server MUST accept responsibility for either delivering the message or properly reporting the failure to do so (see Sections 6.1, 6.2, and 7.8, below).

requirements.heading: Background
requirements.text: Contemporary SMTP implementations MUST support the basic extension mechanisms.

requirements.heading: Background
requirements.text: For instance, servers MUST support the EHLO command even if they do not implement any specific extensions and clients SHOULD preferentially utilize EHLO rather than HELO.

requirements.heading: Background
requirements.text: (However, for compatibility with older conforming implementations, SMTP clients and servers MUST support the original HELO mechanisms as a fallback.) Unless the different characteristics of HELO must be identified for interoperability purposes, this document discusses only EHLO.

requirements.heading: Definition and Registration of Extensions
requirements.text: Keywords beginning with "X" MUST NOT be used in a registered service extension.

requirements.heading: Definition and Registration of Extensions
requirements.text: Conversely, keyword values presented in the EHLO response that do not begin with "X" MUST correspond to a Standard, Standards-Track, or IESG-approved Experimental SMTP service extension registered with IANA.

requirements.heading: Definition and Registration of Extensions
requirements.text: A conforming server MUST NOT offer non-"X"-prefixed keyword values that are not described in a registered extension.

requirements.heading: Special Issues with Extensions
requirements.text: In particular, if an extension implies that the delivery path normally supports special features of that extension, and an intermediate SMTP system finds a next hop that does not support the required extension, it MAY choose, based on the specific extension and circumstances, to requeue the message and try later and/or try an alternate MX host.

requirements.heading: Special Issues with Extensions
requirements.text: If this strategy is employed, the timeout to fall back to an unextended format (if one is available) SHOULD be less than the normal timeout for bouncing as undeliverable (e.g., if normal timeout is three days, the requeue timeout before attempting to transmit the mail without the extension might be one day).

requirements.heading: Host
requirements.text: Hosts are known by names (see the next section); they SHOULD NOT be identified by numerical addresses, i.e., by address literals as described in Section 4.1.2.

requirements.heading: Domain Names
requirements.text: Local aliases MUST NOT appear in any SMTP transaction.

requirements.heading: Domain Names
requirements.text: Local nicknames or unqualified names MUST NOT be used.

requirements.heading: Domain Names
requirements.text: o The domain name given in the EHLO command MUST be either a primary host name (a domain name that resolves to an address RR) or, if the host has no name, an address literal, as described in Section 4.1.3 and discussed further in the EHLO discussion of Section 4.1.4.

requirements.heading: Domain Names
requirements.text: o The reserved mailbox name "postmaster" may be used in a RCPT command without domain qualification (see Section 4.1.1.3) and MUST be accepted if so used.

requirements.heading: Lines
requirements.text: Conforming implementations MUST NOT recognize or generate any other character or character sequence as a line terminator.

requirements.heading: Lines
requirements.text: Limits MAY be imposed on line lengths by servers (see Section 4).

requirements.heading: Lines
requirements.text: SMTP client implementations MUST NOT transmit these characters except when they are intended as line terminators and then MUST, as indicated above, transmit them only as a <CRLF> sequence.

requirements.text: optimize transport by modifying them, the local-part MUST be interpreted and assigned semantics only by the host specified in the domain part of the address.

requirements.heading: General Syntax Principles and Transaction Model
requirements.text: That is, a command verb, an argument value other than a mailbox local-part, and free form text MAY be encoded in upper case, lower case, or any mixture of upper and lower case with no impact on its meaning.

requirements.heading: General Syntax Principles and Transaction Model
requirements.text: The local-part of a mailbox MUST BE treated as case sensitive.

requirements.heading: General Syntax Principles and Transaction Model
requirements.text: Therefore, SMTP implementations MUST take care to preserve the case of mailbox local-parts.

requirements.heading: General Syntax Principles and Transaction Model
requirements.text: Implementations MAY wish to employ this encoding to accommodate those servers.

requirements.heading: General Syntax Principles and Transaction Model
requirements.text: An originating SMTP client that has not successfully negotiated an appropriate extension with a particular server (see the next paragraph) MUST NOT transmit messages with information in the high-order bit of octets.

requirements.heading: General Syntax Principles and Transaction Model
requirements.text: If such messages are transmitted in violation of this rule, receiving SMTP servers MAY clear the high- order bit or reject the message as invalid.

requirements.heading: General Syntax Principles and Transaction Model
requirements.text: In general, a relay SMTP SHOULD assume that the message content it has received is valid and, assuming that the envelope permits doing so, relay it without inspecting that content.

requirements.heading: General Syntax Principles and Transaction Model
requirements.text: Delivery SMTP systems MAY reject such messages, or return them as undeliverable, rather than deliver them.

requirements.heading: General Syntax Principles and Transaction Model
requirements.text: Receiving systems SHOULD reject such commands, normally using "500 syntax error - invalid character" replies.

requirements.heading: General Syntax Principles and Transaction Model
requirements.text: 8-bit message content transmission MAY be requested of the server by a client using extended SMTP facilities, notably the "8BITMIME" extension, RFC 1652 [22].

requirements.heading: General Syntax Principles and Transaction Model
requirements.text: 8BITMIME SHOULD be supported by SMTP servers.

requirements.heading: General Syntax Principles and Transaction Model
requirements.text: However, it MUST NOT be construed as authorization to transmit unrestricted 8-bit material, nor does 8BITMIME authorize transmission of any envelope material in other than ASCII.

requirements.heading: General Syntax Principles and Transaction Model
requirements.text: 8BITMIME MUST NOT be requested by senders for material with the high bit on that is not in MIME format with an appropriate content-transfer encoding; servers MAY reject such messages.

requirements.heading: Session Initiation
requirements.text: SMTP server implementations MAY include identification of their software and version information in the connection greeting reply after the 220 code, a practice that permits more efficient isolation and repair of any problems.

requirements.heading: Session Initiation
requirements.text: Implementations MAY make provision for SMTP servers to disable the software and version announcement where it causes security concerns.

requirements.heading: Session Initiation
requirements.text: The SMTP protocol allows a server to formally reject a mail session while still allowing the initial connection as follows: a 554 response MAY be given in the initial connection opening message instead of the 220.

requirements.heading: Session Initiation
requirements.text: A server taking this approach MUST still wait for the client to send a QUIT (see Section 4.1.1.10) before closing the connection and SHOULD respond to any intervening commands with "503 bad sequence of commands".

requirements.heading: Session Initiation
requirements.text: Since an attempt to make an SMTP connection to such a system is probably in error, a server returning a 554 response on connection opening SHOULD provide enough information in the reply text to facilitate debugging of the sending system.

requirements.heading: Client Initiation
requirements.text: Older SMTP systems that are unable to support service extensions, and contemporary clients that do not require service extensions in the mail session being initiated, MAY use HELO instead of EHLO.

requirements.heading: Client Initiation
requirements.text: Servers MUST NOT return the extended EHLO- style response to a HELO command.

requirements.heading: Client Initiation
requirements.text: For a particular connection attempt, if the server returns a "command not recognized" response to EHLO, the client SHOULD be able to fall back and send HELO.

requirements.heading: Mail Transactions
requirements.text: If the mailbox specification is not acceptable for some reason, the server MUST return a reply indicating whether the failure is permanent (i.e., will occur again if the client tries to send the same address again) or temporary (i.e., the address might be accepted if the client tries again later).

requirements.heading: Mail Transactions
requirements.text: In those cases, the server MAY reasonably accept the reverse-path (with a 250 reply) and then report problems after the forward-paths are received and examined.

requirements.heading: Mail Transactions
requirements.text: Historically, the <reverse-path> was permitted to contain more than just a mailbox; however, contemporary systems SHOULD NOT use source routing (see Appendix C).

requirements.heading: Mail Transactions
requirements.text: Historically, the <forward-path> was permitted to contain a source routing list of hosts and the destination mailbox; however, contemporary SMTP clients SHOULD NOT utilize source routes (see Appendix C).

requirements.heading: Mail Transactions
requirements.text: Servers MUST be prepared to encounter a list of source routes in the forward-path, but they SHOULD ignore the routes or MAY decline to support the relaying they imply.

requirements.heading: Mail Transactions
requirements.text: Similarly, servers MAY decline to accept mail that is destined for other hosts or systems.

requirements.heading: Mail Transactions
requirements.text: Consequently, restricted- capability clients MUST NOT assume that any SMTP server on the Internet can be used as their mail processing (relaying) site.

requirements.heading: Mail Transactions
requirements.text: If a RCPT command appears without a previous MAIL command, the server MUST return a 503 "Bad sequence of commands" response.

requirements.heading: Mail Transactions
requirements.text: If there was no MAIL, or no RCPT, command, or all such commands were rejected, the server MAY return a "command out of sequence" (503) or "no valid recipients" (554) reply in response to the DATA command.

requirements.heading: Mail Transactions
requirements.text: If one of those replies (or any other 5yz reply) is received, the client MUST NOT send the message data; more generally, message data MUST NOT be sent unless a 354 reply is received.

requirements.heading: Mail Transactions
requirements.text: These servers SHOULD treat a failure for one or more recipients as a "subsequent failure" and return a mail message as discussed in Section 6 and, in particular, in Section 6.1.

requirements.heading: Mail Transactions
requirements.text: Server SMTP systems SHOULD NOT reject messages based on perceived defects in the RFC 822 or MIME (RFC 2045 [21]) message header section or message body.

requirements.heading: Mail Transactions
requirements.text: In particular, they MUST NOT reject messages in which the numbers of Resent-header fields do not match or Resent-to appears without Resent-from and/or Resent-date.

requirements.heading: Mail Transactions
requirements.text: Mail transaction commands MUST be used in the order discussed above.

requirements.heading: Forwarding for Address Correction or Updating
requirements.text: o Servers MAY forward messages when they are aware of an address change.

requirements.heading: Forwarding for Address Correction or Updating
requirements.text: When they do so, they MAY either provide address-updating information with a 251 code, or may forward "silently" and return a 250 code.

requirements.heading: Forwarding for Address Correction or Updating
requirements.text: However, if a 251 code is used, they MUST NOT assume that the client will actually update address information or even return that information to the user.

requirements.heading: Forwarding for Address Correction or Updating
requirements.text: o Servers MAY reject messages or return them as non-deliverable when they cannot be delivered precisely as addressed.

requirements.heading: Forwarding for Address Correction or Updating
requirements.text: When they do so, they MAY either provide address-updating information with a 551 code, or may reject the message as undeliverable with a 550 code and no address-specific information.

requirements.heading: Forwarding for Address Correction or Updating
requirements.text: However, if a 551 code is used, they MUST NOT assume that the client will actually update address information or even return that information to the user.

requirements.heading: Forwarding for Address Correction or Updating
requirements.text: SMTP server implementations that support the 251 and/or 551 reply codes SHOULD provide configuration mechanisms so that sites that conclude that they would undesirably disclose information can disable or restrict their use.

requirements.heading: Overview
requirements.text: Implementations SHOULD support VRFY and EXPN (however, see Section 3.5.2 and Section 7.3).

requirements.heading: Overview
requirements.text: If a normal (i.e., 250) response is returned, the response MAY include the full name of the user and MUST include the mailbox of the user.

requirements.heading: Overview
requirements.text: It MUST be in either of the following forms:

requirements.heading: Overview
requirements.text: When a name that is the argument to VRFY could identify more than one mailbox, the server MAY either note the ambiguity or identify the alternatives.

requirements.heading: Overview
requirements.text: For the EXPN command, the string identifies a mailing list, and the successful (i.e., 250) multiline response MAY include the full name of the users and MUST give the mailboxes on the mailing list.

requirements.heading: Overview
requirements.text: If a request is made to apply VRFY to a mailing list, a positive response MAY be given if a message so addressed would be delivered to everyone on the list, otherwise an error SHOULD be reported (e.g., "550 That is a mailing list, not a user" or "252 Unable to verify members of mailing list").

requirements.heading: Overview
requirements.text: If a request is made to expand a user name, the server MAY return a

requirements.heading: Overview
requirements.text: positive response consisting of a list containing one name, or an error MAY be reported (e.g., "550 That is a user name, not a mailing list").

requirements.heading: Overview
requirements.text: An implementation of the VRFY or EXPN commands MUST include at least recognition of local mailboxes as "user names".

requirements.heading: Overview
requirements.text: However, since current Internet practice often results in a single host handling mail for multiple domains, hosts, especially hosts that provide this functionality, SHOULD accept the "local-part@domain" form as a "user name"; hosts MAY also choose to recognize other strings as "user names".

requirements.heading: Overview
requirements.text: Similarly, historical variations in what is returned by these commands are such that the response SHOULD be interpreted very carefully, if at all, and SHOULD generally only be used for diagnostic purposes.

requirements.heading: VRFY Normal Response
requirements.text: When normal (2yz or 551) responses are returned from a VRFY or EXPN request, the reply MUST include the <Mailbox> name using a "<local-part@domain>" construction, where "domain" is a fully- qualified domain name.

requirements.heading: VRFY Normal Response
requirements.text: In circumstances exceptional enough to justify violating the intent of this specification, free-form text MAY be returned.

requirements.heading: VRFY Normal Response
requirements.text: and people, addresses SHOULD appear in pointed brackets.

requirements.heading: VRFY Normal Response
requirements.text: When addresses, rather than free-form debugging information, are returned, EXPN and VRFY MUST return only valid domain addresses that are usable in SMTP RCPT commands.

requirements.heading: VRFY Normal Response
requirements.text: Consequently, if an address implies delivery to a program or other system, the mailbox name used to reach that target MUST be given.

requirements.heading: VRFY Normal Response
requirements.text: Paths (explicit source routes) MUST NOT be returned by VRFY or EXPN.

requirements.heading: VRFY Normal Response
requirements.text: Server implementations SHOULD support both VRFY and EXPN.

requirements.heading: VRFY Normal Response
requirements.text: For security reasons, implementations MAY provide local installations a way to disable either or both of these commands through configuration options or the equivalent (see Section 7.3).

requirements.heading: VRFY Normal Response
requirements.text: Since they were both optional in RFC 821, but VRFY was made mandatory in RFC 1123 [3], if EXPN is supported, it MUST be listed as a service extension in an EHLO response.

requirements.heading: VRFY Normal Response
requirements.text: VRFY MAY be listed as a convenience but, since support for it is required, SMTP clients are not required to check for its presence on the extension list before using it.

requirements.heading: Meaning of VRFY or EXPN Success Response
requirements.text: A server MUST NOT return a 250 code in response to a VRFY or EXPN command unless it has actually verified the address.

requirements.heading: Meaning of VRFY or EXPN Success Response
requirements.text: In particular, a server MUST NOT return 250 if all it has done is to verify that the syntax given is valid.

requirements.heading: Meaning of VRFY or EXPN Success Response
requirements.text: In that case, 502 (Command not implemented) or 500 (Syntax error, command unrecognized) SHOULD be returned.

requirements.heading: Meaning of VRFY or EXPN Success Response
requirements.text: In these situations, reply code 252 SHOULD be returned.

requirements.heading: Meaning of VRFY or EXPN Success Response
requirements.text: Implementations generally SHOULD be more aggressive about address verification in the case of VRFY than in the case of RCPT, even if it takes a little longer to do so.

requirements.heading: Semantics and Applications of EXPN
requirements.text: The propagation of aliasing systems with mail on the Internet for hosts (typically with MX and CNAME DNS records), for mailboxes (various types of local host aliases), and in various proxying arrangements has made it nearly impossible for these strategies to work consistently, and mail systems SHOULD NOT attempt them.

requirements.heading: Source Routes and Relaying
requirements.text: SMTP clients SHOULD NOT generate explicit source routes except under unusual circumstances.

requirements.heading: Source Routes and Relaying
requirements.text: SMTP servers MAY decline to act as mail relays or to accept addresses that specify source routes.

requirements.heading: Source Routes and Relaying
requirements.text: When route information is encountered, SMTP servers MAY ignore the route information and simply send to the final destination specified as the last element in the route and SHOULD do so.

requirements.heading: Source Routes and Relaying
requirements.text: This is one of several reasons why SMTP clients MUST NOT generate invalid source routes or depend on serial resolution of names.

requirements.heading: Mail eXchange Records and Relaying
requirements.text: relay mail to a particular address for policy reasons, a 550 response SHOULD be returned.

requirements.heading: Mail eXchange Records and Relaying
requirements.text: A server MAY attempt to verify the return path before using its address for delivery notifications, but methods of doing so are not defined here nor is any particular method recommended at this time.

requirements.heading: Message Submission Servers as Relays
requirements.text: If an SMTP server has accepted the task of relaying the mail and later finds that the destination is incorrect or that the mail cannot be delivered for some other reason, then it MUST construct an "undeliverable mail" notification message and send it to the originator of the undeliverable mail (as indicated by the reverse- path).

requirements.heading: Message Submission Servers as Relays
requirements.text: Formats specified for non-delivery reports by other standards (see, for example, RFC 3461 [32] and RFC 3464 [33]) SHOULD be used if possible.

requirements.heading: Message Submission Servers as Relays
requirements.text: Of course, SMTP servers MUST NOT send notification messages about problems transporting notification messages.

requirements.heading: Message Submission Servers as Relays
requirements.text: When such a message is transmitted, the reverse-path MUST be set to null (see

requirements.heading: Message Submission Servers as Relays
requirements.text: As discussed in Section 6.4, a relay SMTP has no need to inspect or act upon the header section or body of the message data and MUST NOT do so except to add its own "Received:" header field (Section 4.4) and, optionally, to attempt to detect looping in the mail system (see Section 6.3).

requirements.heading: Header Fields in Gatewaying
requirements.text: Header fields MAY be rewritten when necessary as messages are gatewayed across mail environment boundaries.

requirements.heading: Received Lines in Gatewaying
requirements.text: When forwarding a message into or out of the Internet environment, a gateway MUST prepend a Received: line, but it MUST NOT alter in any way a Received: line that is already in the header section.

requirements.heading: Received Lines in Gatewaying
requirements.text: As another consequence of trace header fields arising in non-SMTP environments, receiving systems MUST NOT reject mail based on the format of a trace header field and SHOULD be extremely robust in the light of unexpected information or formats in those header fields.

requirements.heading: Received Lines in Gatewaying
requirements.text: The gateway SHOULD indicate the environment and protocol in the "via" clauses of Received header field(s) that it supplies.

requirements.heading: Addresses in Gatewaying
requirements.text: From the Internet side, the gateway SHOULD accept all valid address formats in SMTP commands and in the RFC 822 header section, and all valid RFC 822 messages.

requirements.heading: Addresses in Gatewaying
requirements.text: Addresses and header fields generated by gateways MUST conform to applicable standards (including this one and RFC 5322 [4]).

requirements.heading: Other Header Fields in Gatewaying
requirements.text: The gateway MUST ensure that all header fields of a message that it forwards into the Internet mail environment meet the requirements for Internet mail.

requirements.heading: Other Header Fields in Gatewaying
requirements.text: In particular, all addresses in "From:", "To:", "Cc:", etc., header fields MUST be transformed (if necessary) to satisfy the standard header syntax of RFC 5322 [4], MUST reference only fully-qualified domain names, and MUST be effective and useful for sending replies.

requirements.heading: Other Header Fields in Gatewaying
requirements.text: The translation algorithm used to convert mail from the Internet protocols to another environment's protocol SHOULD ensure that error messages from the foreign mail environment are delivered to the reverse-path from the SMTP envelope, not to an address in the "From:", "Sender:", or similar header fields of the message.

requirements.heading: Envelopes in Gatewaying
requirements.text: Similarly, when forwarding a message from another environment into the Internet, the gateway SHOULD set the envelope return path in accordance with an error message return address, if supplied by the foreign environment.

requirements.heading: Terminating Sessions and Connections
requirements.text: An SMTP server MUST NOT intentionally close the connection under normal operational circumstances (see Section 7.8) except:

requirements.heading: Terminating Sessions and Connections
requirements.text: An SMTP server that is forcibly shut down via external means SHOULD attempt to send a line containing a 421 response code to the SMTP client before exiting.

requirements.heading: Terminating Sessions and Connections
requirements.text: SMTP clients that experience a connection close, reset, or other communications failure due to circumstances not under their control (in violation of the intent of this specification but sometimes unavoidable) SHOULD, to maintain the robustness of the mail system, treat the mail transaction as if a 451 response had been received and act accordingly.

requirements.heading: Mailing Lists and Aliases
requirements.text: An SMTP-capable host SHOULD support both the alias and the list models of address expansion for multiple delivery.

requirements.heading: Mailing Lists and Aliases
requirements.text: When a message is delivered or forwarded to each address of an expanded list form, the return address in the envelope ("MAIL FROM:") MUST be changed to be the address of a person or other entity who administers the list.

requirements.heading: Mailing Lists and Aliases
requirements.text: However, in this case, the message header section (RFC 5322 [4]) MUST be left unchanged; in particular, the "From" field of the header section is unaffected.

requirements.heading: Mailing Lists and Aliases
requirements.text: Servers SHOULD simply utilize the addresses on the list; application of heuristics or other matching rules to eliminate some addresses, such as that of the originator, is strongly discouraged.

requirements.heading: Command Semantics and Syntax
requirements.text: (In the interest of improved interoperability, SMTP receivers SHOULD tolerate trailing white space before the terminating <CRLF>.) The syntax of the local part of a mailbox MUST conform to receiver site conventions and the syntax specified in Section 4.1.2.

requirements.heading: Command Semantics and Syntax
requirements.text: In the absence of specific extensions offered by the server and accepted by the client, clients MUST NOT send such parameters and servers SHOULD reject commands containing them as having invalid syntax.

requirements.heading: Extended HELLO (EHLO) or HELLO (HELO)
requirements.text: available), the client SHOULD send an address literal (see Section 4.1.3).

requirements.heading: Extended HELLO (EHLO) or HELLO (HELO)
requirements.text: In the interest of interoperability, it is probably wise for servers to be prepared for this string to occur, but SMTP clients SHOULD NOT send it.

requirements.heading: Extended HELLO (EHLO) or HELLO (HELO)
requirements.text: A client SMTP SHOULD start an SMTP session by issuing the EHLO command.

requirements.heading: Extended HELLO (EHLO) or HELLO (HELO)
requirements.text: Older client SMTP systems MAY, as discussed above, use HELO (as specified in RFC 821) instead of EHLO, and servers MUST support the HELO command and reply properly to it.

requirements.heading: Extended HELLO (EHLO) or HELLO (HELO)
requirements.text: In any event, a client MUST issue HELO or EHLO before starting a mail transaction.

requirements.heading: Extended HELLO (EHLO) or HELLO (HELO)
requirements.text: Although EHLO keywords may be specified in upper, lower, or mixed case, they MUST always be recognized and processed in a case- insensitive manner.

requirements.heading: Extended HELLO (EHLO) or HELLO (HELO)
requirements.text: The EHLO response MUST contain keywords (and associated parameters if required) for all commands not listed as "required" in Section 4.5.1 excepting only private-use commands as described in Section 4.1.5.

requirements.heading: Extended HELLO (EHLO) or HELLO (HELO)
requirements.text: Private-use commands MAY be listed.

requirements.heading: RECIPIENT (RCPT)
requirements.text: Sending systems SHOULD NOT generate the optional list of hosts known as a source route.

requirements.heading: RECIPIENT (RCPT)
requirements.text: Receiving systems MUST recognize source route syntax but SHOULD strip off the source route specification and utilize the domain name associated with the mailbox as if the source route had not been provided.

requirements.heading: RECIPIENT (RCPT)
requirements.text: Similarly, relay hosts SHOULD strip or ignore source routes, and names MUST NOT be copied into the reverse-path.

requirements.heading: RECIPIENT (RCPT)
requirements.text: As provided in Appendix C, xyz.com MAY also choose to relay the message to hosta.int, using the envelope commands

requirements.heading: RECIPIENT (RCPT)
requirements.text: Since hosts are not required to relay mail at all, xyz.com MAY also reject the message entirely when the RCPT command is received, using a 550 code (since this is a "policy reason").

requirements.heading: RECIPIENT (RCPT)
requirements.text: The client MUST NOT transmit parameters other than those associated with a service extension offered by the server in its EHLO response.

requirements.heading: DATA (DATA)
requirements.text: The mail data may contain any of the 128 ASCII character codes, although experience has indicated that use of control characters other than SP, HT, CR, and LF may cause problems and SHOULD be avoided when possible.

requirements.heading: DATA (DATA)
requirements.text: An extra <CRLF> MUST NOT be added, as that would cause an empty line to be added to the message.

requirements.heading: DATA (DATA)
requirements.text: body were passed to the originating SMTP-sender with a final "line" that did not end in <CRLF>; in that case, the originating SMTP system MUST either reject the message as invalid or add <CRLF> in order to have the receiving SMTP server recognize the "end of data" condition.

requirements.heading: DATA (DATA)
requirements.text: The custom of accepting lines ending only in <LF>, as a concession to non-conforming behavior on the part of some UNIX systems, has proven to cause more interoperability problems than it solves, and SMTP server systems MUST NOT do this, even in the name of improved robustness.

requirements.heading: DATA (DATA)
requirements.text: In particular, the sequence "<LF>.<LF>" (bare line feeds, without carriage returns) MUST NOT be treated as equivalent to <CRLF>.<CRLF> as the end of mail data indication.

requirements.heading: DATA (DATA)
requirements.text: If the processing is successful, the receiver MUST send an OK reply.

requirements.heading: DATA (DATA)
requirements.text: If the processing fails, the receiver MUST send a failure reply.

requirements.heading: DATA (DATA)
requirements.text: Errors that are diagnosed subsequently MUST be reported in a mail message, as discussed in Section 4.4.

requirements.heading: RESET (RSET)
requirements.text: Any stored sender, recipients, and mail data MUST be discarded, and all buffers and state tables cleared.

requirements.heading: RESET (RSET)
requirements.text: The receiver MUST send a "250 OK" reply to a RSET command with no arguments.

requirements.heading: RESET (RSET)
requirements.text: An SMTP server MUST NOT close the connection as the result of receiving a RSET; that action is reserved for QUIT (see Section 4.1.1.10).

requirements.heading: RESET (RSET)
requirements.text: To preserve the robustness of the mail system, SMTP servers SHOULD be prepared for this condition and SHOULD treat it as if a QUIT had been received before the connection disappeared.

requirements.heading: HELP (HELP)
requirements.text: The command MAY take an argument (e.g., any command name) and return more specific information as a response.

requirements.heading: HELP (HELP)
requirements.text: SMTP servers SHOULD support HELP without arguments and MAY support it with arguments.

requirements.heading: NOOP (NOOP)
requirements.text: If a parameter string is specified, servers SHOULD ignore it.

requirements.heading: QUIT (QUIT)
requirements.text: This command specifies that the receiver MUST send a "221 OK" reply, and then close the transmission channel.

requirements.heading: QUIT (QUIT)
requirements.text: The receiver MUST NOT intentionally close the transmission channel until it receives and replies to a QUIT command (even if there was an error).

requirements.heading: QUIT (QUIT)
requirements.text: The sender MUST NOT intentionally close the transmission channel until it sends a QUIT command, and it SHOULD wait until it receives the reply (even if there was an error response to a previous command).

requirements.heading: QUIT (QUIT)
requirements.text: If the connection is closed prematurely due to violations of the above or system or network failure, the server MUST cancel any pending transaction, but not undo any previously completed transaction, and generally MUST act as if the command or transaction in progress had received a temporary error (i.e., a 4yz response).

requirements.heading: Order of Commands
requirements.text: A session that will contain mail transactions MUST first be initialized by the use of the EHLO command.

requirements.heading: Order of Commands
requirements.text: An SMTP server SHOULD accept commands for non-mail transactions (e.g., VRFY or EXPN) without this initialization.

requirements.heading: Order of Commands
requirements.text: An EHLO command MAY be issued by a client later in the session.

requirements.heading: Order of Commands
requirements.text: If it is issued after the session begins and the EHLO command is acceptable to the SMTP server, the SMTP server MUST clear all buffers and reset the state exactly as if a RSET command had been issued.

requirements.heading: Order of Commands

requirements.heading: Order of Commands

requirements.heading: Order of Commands
requirements.text: An SMTP server MAY verify that the domain name argument in the EHLO command actually corresponds to the IP address of the client.

requirements.heading: Order of Commands
requirements.text: However, if the verification fails, the server MUST NOT refuse to accept a message on that basis.

requirements.heading: Order of Commands

requirements.heading: Order of Commands

requirements.text: When an SMTP server returns a temporary error status (4yz) code after the DATA command is completed with <CRLF>.<CRLF>, it MUST NOT make a subsequent attempt to deliver that message.

requirements.heading: Reply Codes after DATA and the Subsequent <CRLF>.<CRLF>
requirements.text: The user who originated the message SHOULD be able to interpret the return of a transient failure status (by mail message or otherwise) as a non-delivery indication, just as a permanent failure would be interpreted.

requirements.heading: Reply Codes after DATA and the Subsequent <CRLF>.<CRLF>
requirements.text: When an SMTP server returns a permanent error status (5yz) code after the DATA command is completed with <CRLF>.<CRLF>, it MUST NOT make any subsequent attempt to deliver the message.

requirements.text: As with temporary error status codes, the SMTP client retains responsibility for the message, but SHOULD not again attempt delivery to the same server without user review of the message and response and appropriate intervention.

requirements.heading: Command-Reply Sequences
requirements.text: Unless extended using the mechanisms described in Section 2.2, SMTP servers MUST NOT transmit reply codes to an SMTP client that are other than three digits or that do not start in a digit between 2 and 5 inclusive.

requirements.heading: Command-Reply Sequences
requirements.text: However, if the target is more precise granularity in the codes, rather than codes for completely new purposes, the system described in RFC 3463 [25] SHOULD be used in preference to the invention of new codes.

requirements.heading: Command-Reply Sequences

requirements.heading: Trace Information
requirements.text: When an SMTP server receives a message for delivery or further processing, it MUST insert trace ("time stamp" or "Received") information at the beginning of the message content, as discussed in Section 4.1.1.4.

requirements.heading: Trace Information
requirements.text: This line MUST be structured as follows:

requirements.heading: Trace Information
requirements.text: o The FROM clause, which MUST be supplied in an SMTP environment, SHOULD contain both (1) the name of the source host as presented in the EHLO command and (2) an address literal containing the IP address of the source, determined from the TCP connection.

requirements.heading: Trace Information
requirements.text: o The ID clause MAY contain an "@" as suggested in RFC 822, but this is not required.

requirements.heading: Trace Information
requirements.text: o If the FOR clause appears, it MUST contain exactly one <path> entry, even when multiple RCPT commands have been given.

requirements.heading: Trace Information
requirements.text: An Internet mail program MUST NOT change or delete a Received: line that was previously added to the message header section.

requirements.heading: Trace Information
requirements.text: SMTP servers MUST prepend Received lines to messages; they MUST NOT change the order of existing lines or insert Received lines in any other location.

requirements.heading: Trace Information
requirements.text: SMTP servers that create Received header fields SHOULD use explicit offsets in the dates (e.g., -0800), rather than time zone names of any type.

requirements.heading: Trace Information
requirements.text: Local time (with an offset) SHOULD be used rather than UT when feasible.

requirements.heading: Trace Information
requirements.text: If it is desired to supply a time zone name, it SHOULD be included in a comment.

requirements.heading: Trace Information
requirements.text: This use of return-path is required; mail systems MUST support it.

requirements.heading: Trace Information
requirements.text: Consequently, any further (forwarding, gateway, or relay) systems MAY remove the return path and rebuild the MAIL command as needed to ensure that exactly one such line appears in a delivered message.

requirements.heading: Trace Information
requirements.text: A message-originating SMTP system SHOULD NOT send a message that already contains a Return-path header field.

requirements.heading: Trace Information
requirements.text: SMTP servers performing a relay function MUST NOT inspect the message data, and especially not to the extent needed to determine if Return-path header fields are present.

requirements.heading: Trace Information
requirements.text: SMTP servers making final delivery MAY remove Return- path header fields before adding their own.

requirements.heading: Trace Information
requirements.text: For this to be unambiguous, exactly one return path SHOULD be present when the message is delivered.

requirements.heading: Trace Information
requirements.text: Systems using RFC 822 syntax with non-SMTP transports SHOULD designate an unambiguous address, associated with the transport envelope, to which error reports (e.g., non-delivery messages) should be sent.

requirements.heading: Trace Information
requirements.text: The reverse-path address (as copied into the Return-path) MUST be used as the target of any mail containing delivery error messages.

requirements.heading: Trace Information
requirements.text: In particular: o a gateway from SMTP -> elsewhere SHOULD insert a return-path header field, unless it is known that the "elsewhere" transport also uses Internet domain addresses and maintains the envelope sender address separately.

requirements.heading: Trace Information
requirements.text: o a gateway from elsewhere -> SMTP SHOULD delete any return-path header field present in the message, and either copy that information to the SMTP envelope or combine it with information present in the envelope of the other transport system to construct the reverse-path argument to the MAIL command in the SMTP envelope.

requirements.heading: Trace Information
requirements.text: In such cases, the response to the DATA command MUST be an OK reply.

requirements.heading: Trace Information
requirements.text: However, the SMTP server MUST compose and send an "undeliverable mail" notification message to the originator of the message.

requirements.heading: Trace Information
requirements.text: A single notification listing all of the failed recipients or separate notification messages MUST be sent for each failed recipient.

requirements.heading: Trace Information
requirements.text: For economy of processing by the sender, the former SHOULD be used when possible.

requirements.heading: Trace Information
requirements.text: All notification messages about undeliverable mail MUST be sent using the MAIL command (even if they result from processing the obsolete SEND, SOML, or SAML commands) and MUST use a null return path as discussed in Section 3.6.

requirements.heading: Minimum Implementation
requirements.text: In order to make SMTP workable, the following minimum implementation MUST be provided by all receivers.

requirements.heading: Minimum Implementation
requirements.text: The following commands MUST be supported to conform to this specification:

requirements.heading: Minimum Implementation
requirements.text: Any system that includes an SMTP server supporting mail relaying or delivery MUST support the reserved mailbox "postmaster" as a case- insensitive local name.

requirements.heading: Minimum Implementation
requirements.text: The requirement to accept mail for postmaster implies that RCPT commands that specify a mailbox for postmaster at any of the domains for which the SMTP server provides mail service, as well as the special case of "RCPT TO:<Postmaster>" (with no domain specification), MUST be supported.

requirements.heading: Minimum Implementation
requirements.text: However, such arrangements SHOULD be narrowly tailored so as to avoid blocking messages that are not part of such attacks.

requirements.heading: Transparency
requirements.text: If such transformations are necessary, they MUST be reversible, especially if they are applied to mail being relayed.

requirements.heading: Size Limits and Minimums
requirements.text: Every implementation MUST be able to receive objects of at least these sizes.

requirements.heading: Size Limits and Minimums
requirements.text: Objects larger than these sizes SHOULD be avoided when possible.

requirements.heading: Size Limits and Minimums
requirements.text: Clients MAY attempt to transmit these, but MUST be prepared for a server to reject them if they cannot be handled by it.

requirements.heading: Message Content
requirements.text: The maximum total length of a message content (including any message header section as well as the message body) MUST BE at least 64K octets.

requirements.heading: Message Content
requirements.text: SMTP server systems that must impose restrictions SHOULD implement the "SIZE" service extension of RFC 1870 [10], and SMTP client systems that will send large messages SHOULD utilize it when possible.

requirements.heading: Recipients Buffer
requirements.text: The minimum total number of recipients that MUST be buffered is 100 recipients.

requirements.heading: Recipients Buffer
requirements.text: The general principle that relaying SMTP server MUST NOT, and delivery SMTP servers SHOULD NOT, perform validation tests on message header fields suggests that messages SHOULD NOT be rejected based on the total number of recipients shown in header fields.

requirements.heading: Recipients Buffer
requirements.text: A server that imposes a limit on the number of recipients MUST behave in an orderly fashion, such as rejecting additional addresses over its limit rather than silently discarding addresses previously accepted.

requirements.heading: Recipients Buffer
requirements.text: A client that needs to deliver a message containing over 100 RCPT commands SHOULD be prepared to transmit in 100-recipient "chunks" if the server declines to accept more than 100 recipients in a single message.

requirements.heading: Too Many Recipients Code
requirements.text: Clients SHOULD treat a 552 code in this case as a temporary, rather than permanent, failure so the logic below works.

requirements.heading: Too Many Recipients Code
requirements.text: If an SMTP server has an implementation limit on the number of RCPT commands and this limit is exhausted, it MUST use a response code of 452 (but the client SHOULD also be prepared for a 552, as noted above).

requirements.heading: Too Many Recipients Code
requirements.text: If the server has a configured site-policy limitation on the number of RCPT commands, it MAY instead use a 5yz response code.

requirements.heading: Timeouts
requirements.text: An SMTP client MUST provide a timeout mechanism.

requirements.heading: Timeouts
requirements.text: It MUST use per- command timeouts rather than somehow trying to time the entire mail transaction.

requirements.heading: Timeouts
requirements.text: Timeouts SHOULD be easily reconfigurable, preferably without recompiling the SMTP code.

requirements.heading: Timeouts
requirements.text: Based on extensive experience with busy mail-relay hosts, the minimum per-command timeout values SHOULD be as follows:

requirements.heading: Server Timeout: 5 Minutes.
requirements.text: An SMTP server SHOULD have a timeout of at least 5 minutes while it is awaiting the next command from the sender.

requirements.heading: Retry Strategies
requirements.text: Any queuing strategy MUST include timeouts on all activities on a per-command basis.

requirements.heading: Retry Strategies
requirements.text: A queuing strategy MUST NOT send error messages in response to error messages under any circumstances.

requirements.heading: Sending Strategy
requirements.text: In a typical system, the program that composes a message has some method for requesting immediate attention for a new piece of outgoing mail, while mail that cannot be transmitted immediately MUST be queued and periodically retried by the sender.

requirements.heading: Sending Strategy
requirements.text: The sender MUST delay retrying a particular destination after one attempt has failed.

requirements.heading: Sending Strategy
requirements.text: In general, the retry interval SHOULD be at least 30 minutes; however, more sophisticated and variable strategies will be beneficial when the SMTP client can determine the reason for non-delivery.

requirements.heading: Sending Strategy
requirements.text: It MAY be appropriate to set a shorter maximum number of retries for non- delivery notifications and equivalent error messages than for standard messages.

requirements.heading: Sending Strategy
requirements.text: The parameters to the retry algorithm MUST be configurable.

requirements.heading: Sending Strategy
requirements.text: A client SHOULD keep a list of hosts it cannot reach and corresponding connection timeouts, rather than just retrying queued mail items.

requirements.heading: Sending Strategy
requirements.text: At the same time, SMTP clients SHOULD use great care in caching negative responses from servers.

requirements.heading: Sending Strategy
requirements.text: More significantly, 5yz responses to the MAIL command MUST NOT be cached.

requirements.heading: Sending Strategy
requirements.text: When a mail message is to be delivered to multiple recipients, and the SMTP server to which a copy of the message is to be sent is the same for multiple recipients, then only one copy of the message SHOULD be transmitted.

requirements.heading: Sending Strategy
requirements.text: That is, the SMTP client SHOULD use the command sequence: MAIL, RCPT, RCPT, ..., RCPT, DATA instead of the sequence: MAIL, RCPT, DATA, ..., MAIL, RCPT, DATA.

requirements.heading: Sending Strategy
requirements.text: However, if there are very many addresses, a limit on the number of RCPT commands per MAIL command MAY be imposed.

requirements.heading: Sending Strategy
requirements.text: This efficiency feature SHOULD be implemented.

requirements.heading: Sending Strategy
requirements.text: Similarly, to achieve timely delivery, the SMTP client MAY support multiple concurrent outgoing mail transactions.

requirements.heading: Receiving Strategy
requirements.text: The SMTP server SHOULD attempt to keep a pending listen on the SMTP port (specified by IANA as port 25) at all times.

requirements.heading: Receiving Strategy
requirements.text: Some limit MAY be imposed, but servers that cannot handle more than one SMTP transaction at a time are not in conformance with the intent of this specification.

requirements.heading: Messages with a Null Reverse-Path
requirements.text: All other types of messages (i.e., any message which is not required by a Standards-Track RFC to have a null reverse-path) SHOULD be sent with a valid, non-null reverse-path.

requirements.heading: Messages with a Null Reverse-Path
requirements.text: In particular, such systems SHOULD NOT reply to messages with a null reverse-path, and they SHOULD NOT add a non-null reverse-path, or change a null reverse-path to a non-null one, to such messages when forwarding.

requirements.heading: Locating the Target Host
requirements.text: Once an SMTP client lexically identifies a domain to which mail will be delivered for processing (as described in Sections 2.3.5 and 3.6), a DNS lookup MUST be performed to resolve the domain name (RFC 1035 [2]).

requirements.heading: Locating the Target Host
requirements.text: Due to a history of problems, SMTP servers used for initial submission of messages SHOULD NOT make such inferences (Message Submission Servers [18] have somewhat more flexibility) and intermediate (relay) SMTP servers MUST NOT make them.

requirements.heading: Locating the Target Host
requirements.text: If a non-existent domain error is returned, this situation MUST be reported as an error.

requirements.heading: Locating the Target Host
requirements.text: If a temporary error is returned, the message MUST be queued and retried later (see Section 4.5.4.1).

requirements.heading: Locating the Target Host
requirements.text: If MX records are present, but none of them are usable, or the implicit MX is unusable, this situation MUST be reported as an error.

requirements.heading: Locating the Target Host
requirements.text: If one or more MX RRs are found for a given name, SMTP systems MUST NOT utilize any address RRs associated with that name unless they are located using the MX RRs; the "implicit MX" rule above applies only if there are no MX records present.

requirements.heading: Locating the Target Host
requirements.text: If MX records are present, but none of them are usable, this situation MUST be reported as an error.

requirements.heading: Locating the Target Host
requirements.text: When a domain name associated with an MX RR is looked up and the associated data field obtained, the data field of that response MUST contain a domain name.

requirements.heading: Locating the Target Host
requirements.text: That domain name, when queried, MUST return at least one address record (e.g., A or AAAA RR) that gives the IP address of the SMTP server to which the message should be directed.

requirements.heading: Locating the Target Host
requirements.text: To provide reliable mail transmission, the SMTP client MUST be able to try (and retry) each of the relevant addresses in this list in order, until a delivery attempt succeeds.

requirements.heading: Locating the Target Host
requirements.text: However, there MAY also be a configurable limit on the number of alternate addresses that can be tried.

requirements.heading: Locating the Target Host
requirements.text: In any case, the SMTP client SHOULD try at least two addresses.

requirements.heading: Locating the Target Host
requirements.text: MX records contain a preference indication that MUST be used in sorting if more than one such record appears (see below).

requirements.heading: Locating the Target Host
requirements.text: If there are multiple destinations with the same preference and there is no clear reason to favor one (e.g., by recognition of an easily reached address), then the sender-SMTP MUST randomize them to spread the load across multiple mail exchangers for a specific organization.

requirements.heading: Locating the Target Host
requirements.text: It is the responsibility of the domain name resolver interface to have ordered this list by decreasing preference if necessary, and the SMTP sender MUST try them in the order presented.

requirements.heading: Locating the Target Host
requirements.text: If an SMTP server receives a message with a destination for which it is a designated Mail eXchanger, it MAY relay the message (potentially after having rewritten the MAIL FROM and/or RCPT TO addresses), make final delivery of the message, or hand it off using some mechanism outside the SMTP-provided transport environment.

requirements.heading: Locating the Target Host
requirements.text: If it determines that it should relay the message without rewriting the address, it MUST sort the MX records to determine candidates for

requirements.heading: Locating the Target Host
requirements.text: The relay host MUST then inspect the list for any of the names or addresses by which it might be known in mail transactions.

requirements.heading: Locating the Target Host
requirements.text: If a matching record is found, all records at that preference level and higher-numbered ones MUST be discarded from consideration.

requirements.heading: Locating the Target Host
requirements.text: If there are no records left at that point, it is an error condition, and the message MUST be returned as undeliverable.

requirements.heading: Locating the Target Host
requirements.text: If records do remain, they SHOULD be tried, best preference first, as described above.

requirements.heading: Reliable Delivery and Replies by Email
requirements.text: It MUST NOT lose the message for frivolous reasons, such as because the host later crashes or because of a predictable resource shortage.

requirements.heading: Reliable Delivery and Replies by Email
requirements.text: If there is a delivery failure after acceptance of a message, the receiver-SMTP MUST formulate and mail a notification message.

requirements.heading: Reliable Delivery and Replies by Email
requirements.text: This notification MUST be sent using a null ("<>") reverse-path in the envelope.

requirements.heading: Reliable Delivery and Replies by Email
requirements.text: The recipient of this notification MUST be the address from the envelope return path (or the Return-Path: line).

requirements.heading: Reliable Delivery and Replies by Email
requirements.text: if this address is null ("<>"), the receiver-SMTP MUST NOT send a notification.

requirements.heading: Reliable Delivery and Replies by Email
requirements.text: If the address is an explicit source route, it MUST be stripped down to its final hop.

requirements.heading: Reliable Delivery and Replies by Email
requirements.text: The notification message MUST be sent using:

requirements.heading: Reliable Delivery and Replies by Email
requirements.text: To avoid receiving duplicate messages as the result of timeouts, a receiver-SMTP MUST seek to minimize the time required to respond to the final <CRLF>.<CRLF> end of data indicator.

requirements.heading: Unwanted, Unsolicited, and "Attack" Messages
requirements.text: Reliably determining that a return address is invalid can be a difficult and time-consuming process, especially if the putative sending system is not directly accessible or does not fully and accurately support VRFY and, even if a "drop messages with invalid return addresses" policy is adopted, it SHOULD be applied only when there is near-certainty that the return addresses are, in fact, invalid.

requirements.heading: Unwanted, Unsolicited, and "Attack" Messages
requirements.text: Conversely, if a message is rejected because it is found to contain hostile content (a decision that is outside the scope of an SMTP server as defined in this document), rejection ("bounce") messages SHOULD NOT be sent unless the receiving site is confident that those messages will be usefully delivered.

requirements.heading: Loop Detection
requirements.text: SMTP servers using this technique SHOULD use a large rejection threshold, normally at least 100 Received entries.

requirements.heading: Loop Detection
requirements.text: Whatever mechanisms are used, servers MUST contain provisions for detecting and stopping trivial loops.

requirements.heading: Compensating for Irregularities
requirements.text: The following changes to a message being processed MAY be applied when necessary by an originating SMTP server, or one used as the target of SMTP as an initial posting (message submission) protocol:

requirements.heading: Compensating for Irregularities
requirements.text: These changes MUST NOT be applied by an SMTP server that provides an intermediate relay function.

requirements.heading: Compensating for Irregularities
requirements.text: In all cases, documentation SHOULD be provided in trace header fields and/or header field comments for actions performed by the servers.

requirements.heading: "Blind" Copies
requirements.text: Especially when more than one RCPT command is present, and in order to avoid defeating some of the purpose of these mechanisms, SMTP clients and servers SHOULD NOT copy the full set of RCPT command arguments into the header section, either as part of trace header fields or as informational or private- extension header fields.

requirements.heading: "Blind" Copies
requirements.text: Since this rule is often violated in practice, and cannot be enforced, sending SMTP systems that are aware of "bcc" use MAY find it helpful to send each blind copy as a separate message transaction containing only a single RCPT command.

requirements.heading: "Blind" Copies
requirements.text: Receiving systems SHOULD NOT attempt to deduce such relationships and use them to alter the header section of the message for delivery.

requirements.heading: "Blind" Copies
requirements.text: The popular "Apparently-to" header field is a violation of this principle as well as a common source of unintended information disclosure and SHOULD NOT be used.

requirements.heading: VRFY, EXPN, and Security
requirements.text: As a corollary to the above, implementations that permit this MUST NOT appear to have verified addresses that are not, in fact, verified.

requirements.heading: VRFY, EXPN, and Security
requirements.text: If a site disables these commands for security reasons, the SMTP server MUST return a 252 response, rather than a code that could be confused with successful or unsuccessful verification.

requirements.heading: VRFY, EXPN, and Security
requirements.text: Implementations SHOULD still provide support for EXPN, but sites SHOULD carefully evaluate the tradeoffs.

requirements.heading: Information Disclosure in Announcements
requirements.text: Sites are encouraged to evaluate the tradeoff with that issue in mind; implementations SHOULD minimally provide for making type and version information available in some way to other network hosts.

requirements.heading: Scope of Operation of SMTP Servers
requirements.text: Some sites have decided to limit the use of the relay function to known or identifiable sources, and implementations SHOULD provide the capability to perform this type of filtering.

requirements.heading: Scope of Operation of SMTP Servers
requirements.text: When mail is rejected for these or other policy reasons, a 550 code SHOULD be used in response to EHLO (or HELO), MAIL, or RCPT as appropriate.

requirements.heading: IANA Considerations
requirements.text: In addition, if additional trace header fields (i.e., in addition to Return-path and Received) are ever created, those trace fields MUST be added to the IANA registry established by BCP 90 (RFC 3864) [11] for use with RFC 5322 [4].

requirements.heading: Informative References
requirements.text: However, if the envelope is not supplied, SMTP commands SHOULD be generated as follows:

requirements.heading: Informative References
requirements.text: Each recipient address from a TO, CC, or BCC header field SHOULD be copied to a RCPT command (generating multiple message copies if that is required for queuing or delivery).

requirements.heading: Informative References
requirements.text: Any BCC header fields SHOULD then be removed from the header section.

requirements.heading: Informative References
requirements.text: Once this process is completed, the remaining header fields SHOULD be checked to verify that at least one TO, CC, or BCC header field remains.

requirements.heading: Informative References
requirements.text: If none do, then a BCC header field with no additional information SHOULD be inserted as specified in [4].

requirements.heading: Informative References
requirements.text: The return address in the MAIL command SHOULD, if possible, be derived from the system's identity for the submitting (local) user, and the "From:" header field otherwise.

requirements.heading: Informative References
requirements.text: If there is a system identity available, it SHOULD also be copied to the Sender header field if it is different from the address in the From header field.

requirements.heading: Informative References
requirements.text: (Any Sender header field that was already there SHOULD be removed.) Systems may provide a way for submitters to override the envelope return address, but may want to restrict its use to privileged users.

requirements.heading: Informative References
requirements.text: A submission protocol based on Standard RFC 822 information alone MUST NOT be used to gateway a message from a foreign (non-SMTP) mail system into an SMTP environment.

requirements.heading: Informative References
requirements.text: The first host in the <reverse-path> was historically the host sending the MAIL command; today, source routes SHOULD NOT appear in the reverse-path.

requirements.heading: Informative References
requirements.text: However, in general, the <forward-path> SHOULD contain only a mailbox and domain name, relying on the domain name system to supply routing information if required.

requirements.heading: Informative References
requirements.text: The use of source routes is deprecated (see Appendix F.2); while servers MUST be prepared to receive and handle them as discussed in Section 3.3 and Appendix F.2, clients SHOULD NOT transmit them and this section is included in the current specification only to provide context.

requirements.heading: Informative References
requirements.text: For relay purposes, the forward-path may be a source route of the form "@ONE,@TWO:JOE@THREE", where ONE, TWO, and THREE MUST be fully- qualified domain names.

requirements.heading: Informative References
requirements.text: A server that is reached by means of a source route (e.g., its domain name appears first in the list in the forward-path) MUST remove its domain name from any forward-paths in which that domain name appears before forwarding the message and MAY remove all other source routing information.

requirements.heading: Informative References
requirements.text: The reverse-path SHOULD NOT be updated by servers conforming to this specification.

requirements.heading: Informative References
requirements.text: Conversely, SMTP servers MUST NOT derive final message routing information from message header fields.

requirements.heading: Informative References
requirements.text: If, contrary to the recommendations here, a relay host adds itself to the beginning of the list, it MUST use its name as known in the transport environment to which it is relaying the mail rather than that of the transport environment from which the mail came (if they are different).

requirements.heading: Informative References
requirements.text: This is another reason why servers needing to return a message SHOULD ignore the source route entirely and simply use the domain as specified in the Mailbox.

requirements.heading: Informative References
requirements.text: In general, gateways between the Internet and other mail systems SHOULD attempt to preserve any layering semantics across the boundaries between the two mail systems involved.

requirements.heading: Informative References
requirements.text: A few features of RFC 821 have proven to be problematic and SHOULD NOT be used in Internet mail.

requirements.heading: Informative References
requirements.text: Its use is deprecated; SMTP systems SHOULD NOT use it unless the server can authenticate the client.

requirements.heading: Informative References
requirements.text: SMTP servers MUST continue to accept source route syntax as specified in the main body of this document and in RFC 1123.

requirements.heading: Informative References
requirements.text: They MAY, if necessary, ignore the routes and utilize only the target domain in the address.

requirements.heading: Informative References
requirements.text: If they do utilize the source route, the message MUST be sent to the first domain shown in the address.

requirements.heading: Informative References
requirements.text: In particular, a server MUST NOT guess at shortcuts within the source route.

requirements.heading: Informative References
requirements.text: Clients SHOULD NOT utilize explicit source routing except under unusual circumstances, such as debugging or potentially relaying around firewall or mail system configuration errors.

requirements.heading: Informative References
requirements.text: As discussed in Sections 3.1 and 4.1.1, EHLO SHOULD be used rather than HELO when the server will accept the former.

requirements.heading: Informative References
requirements.text: Servers MUST continue to accept and process HELO in order to support older clients.

requirements.heading: Informative References
requirements.text: It is deprecated and MUST NOT be used.

requirements.heading: Informative References
requirements.text: When dates are inserted into messages by SMTP clients or servers (e.g., in trace header fields), four-digit years MUST BE used.

requirements.heading: Informative References
requirements.text: Clients SHOULD NOT provide SEND, SAML, or SOML as services.

requirements.heading: Informative References
requirements.text: Servers MAY implement them.

requirements.heading: Informative References
requirements.text: If they are implemented by servers, the implementation model specified in RFC 821 MUST be used and the command names MUST be published in the response to the EHLO command.
